lines: Two hundred dollars a month, starting at age 25.
Over forty years, that habit could grow to more than half a million dollars.
Start the very same habit ten years later, and the result drops by more than half.
In the next six minutes, I will show you the math, the catch, and what to do with your own numbers.
First, the rules of this thought experiment.
You save two hundred dollars every month, which adds up to $2,400 a year.
We assume the money earns 7 percent a year, and we ignore taxes and fees.
Real returns change from year to year, and they can be negative, so treat every number here as an illustration.
The point is to see the shape of the curve, not to predict your future.
Before the math, let's see where young adults stand today.
In 2025, the Federal Reserve asked people who are not retired whether their retirement saving was on track.
Overall, 35 percent said yes.
Among adults aged 18 to 29, only 22 percent said yes, and 38 percent had a tax-preferred retirement account.
Starting early is still uncommon, which is a big reason it matters.
Now imagine you keep that $200 in an ordinary savings account.
The FDIC reported a national average savings rate of 0.38 percent in October 2026.
If that rate never changed, forty years of deposits would grow to about $103,700, and $96,000 of it is simply your own money.
That is a fine place for emergency cash.
But it shows why the rate you earn matters almost as much as the amount you save.
So how can the same $200 grow so much more?
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau describes compound interest as earning interest on your savings and on the interest you already earned.
Its example is $1,000 at 5 percent.
After year one you have $1,050, and after year two you have $1,102.50.
That extra $2.50 is interest earning interest, and over decades it snowballs.
Now run our plan from age 25 to age 65.
You would deposit $96,000 over forty years.
At an assumed 7 percent, the balance would be roughly $525,000.
That means about $429,000 came from growth, not from your paycheck.
Notice that most of that growth arrives in the final decade.
Now suppose you wait until 35 and save the same $200 a month for thirty years.
You would deposit $72,000, which is only $24,000 less.
But the balance would be roughly $244,000.
Waiting ten years cost about $281,000 in this example, even though you skipped just $24,000 of deposits.
Time in the account did the heavy lifting, not the size of the monthly payment.
Wait until 45, and twenty years of saving would give you about $104,000.
To reach the same $525,000 from age 45, you would need to save about $1,000 a month.
Late starters are not doomed, but they have to save much more to close the gap.
Here is the catch, and it is a human one.
In the first five years, you would deposit $12,000, and the balance would be about $14,300.
Only around $2,300 of that is growth, which can feel like nothing.
Many people lose motivation in the part of the curve that looks the flattest.
The curve only bends upward after you have been patient for a decade or two.
So where could this money live?
In the United States, a traditional or Roth IRA is a tax-preferred retirement account.
The IRS says that for people under 50, the contribution limit is $7,500 in 2026, up from $7,000 in 2025.
Our $2,400 a year fits well inside that limit.
If your employer offers a 401(k), ask whether it comes with a match.
One warning before you invest every spare dollar.
The Fed found that 55 percent of adults had set aside three months of expenses in a rainy day fund.
For adults aged 18 to 29, the number was 37 percent.
Without a cushion, a surprise bill can force you to pull money out early and break the chain.
So many people build a small emergency fund first, and then add the long-term habit.
Maybe $200 is not realistic for you right now, and that is fine.
The Fed found that only 7 percent of non-retirees with family income under $25,000 felt on track, compared with 59 percent at $100,000 or more.
Income matters, so be honest about your budget.
The math scales: $50 a month from age 25 would become roughly a quarter of our result, about $131,000.
Start with an amount you can keep, and raise it whenever your pay goes up.
So what did two hundred dollars a month actually buy?
Starting at 25, it turned $96,000 of deposits into roughly $525,000 in our illustration.
At 35, the same monthly habit reached about $244,000, and at 45, about $104,000.
The lesson is simple: the earlier the first deposit, the more years do the work for you.
Real returns will differ, so use these numbers as a map, not a promise.
